summary.text: Faraday's law of induction describes how a changing magnetic field can drive an electric current in a circuit.
In its flux-rule form, the emf around a closed loop equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through it.
This is the working principle behind transformers, inductors, and many motors, generators and solenoids.

facts.label: Key experiment
facts.value: Faraday's iron ring with two coils, August 29, 1831

facts.label: Flux rule causes
facts.value: Changing field, moving circuit, or a deformed loop shape

facts.label: Neumann's contribution
facts.value: Set out the math of induction in 1845

facts.label: Static magnets
facts.value: A magnet resting near a loop produces no current

items.prompt: A magnet is held still next to a loop of wire. Which change would produce a current?

options.label: Leaving the magnet exactly where it is
Making the magnet look shinier
Waiting longer
Moving the magnet toward the loop

items.explain: A static field has no effect on a circuit. A changing field, such as one from a moving magnet, induces current.

items.prompt: A flat wire loop is squeezed into a narrower shape inside a steady magnetic field. Does it get an emf?

options.label: Yes, because deforming the loop changes the flux through it
No, because the field never changed
No, because only magnets can cause an emf
Yes, but only if the loop heats up

items.explain: The flux rule accounts for flux changes from field variation, movement of the circuit, or deformation of its shape.

items.prompt: A loop moves through a steady magnetic field and a current appears. Which mechanism is at work?

options.label: Transformer emf from a changing field
Motional emf from the magnetic force on charges
Static charge left on the wire
Heat flowing along the wire

items.explain: In motional emf the circuit moves through a field and the magnetic part of the Lorentz force pushes the charges.

items.prompt: The minus sign in Faraday's law carries which idea?

options.label: The current can never be negative
The induced current's field opposes the change in flux
The loop must be turned upside down
The flux always shrinks

items.explain: The direction is given by Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in the original flux.

items.prompt: Why did the 1831 experiment need a battery to be switched on or off, rather than just connected?

options.label: The meter only works at night
A steady current would have burned out the meter
Changing current in coil one made a changing field in the ring
Batteries only work when moving

items.explain: Faraday concluded that a changing current made a changing magnetic field in the ring, which induced a current in the second coil.

items.prompt: Early critics doubted Faraday's explanation. What was their main objection?

options.label: His experiments never worked
His lines of force had no mathematical form
He used the wrong metal
He copied Henry's results

items.explain: His theoretical ideas met skepticism because they were not formulated mathematically; Maxwell later supplied the math.
